Gun legislation: tables and bibliographic integrity in a RAND report

Source: vignettes/gun-legislation.Rmd
gun-legislation.Rmd
library(bst260projhelp)

This vignette works through RAND’s The Science of Gun Policy (4th ed., 2024), a 512-page report bundled with the package:

pdf <- bst260_example("scienceOfGunPolicy.pdf")

It demonstrates the two kinds of information transformation this package supports on reports like this one – pulling structured tables out of a PDF that was never designed to be machine-read, and recovering enough of the document’s bibliographic structure to check that an in-text claim traces back to a real, identifiable source.

Information transformation: recovering tables from PDF geometry

pdftools::pdf_text() returns each page as a block of plain text, which is enough for prose but loses column structure whenever cells wrap or headers are centred rather than left-aligned – both common in this report. pdf_read_table() instead works from word-level coordinates (pdftools::pdf_data()), grouping words first into text lines and then into columns.

Before parsing an unfamiliar table, find out which page its caption is on:

idx <- pdf_table_index(pdf)
head(idx)
#>   table pdf_page continued
#> 1   S.1       10     FALSE
#> 2   S.1       11      TRUE
#> 3   S.1       12      TRUE
#> 4   2.1       59     FALSE
#> 5   2.2       60     FALSE
#> 6   2.3       69     FALSE
subset(idx, table %in% c("18.1", "A.3", "A.6"))
#>    table pdf_page continued
#> 13  18.1      397     FALSE
#> 21   A.3      492     FALSE
#> 27   A.6      501     FALSE

A simple two-column table: 18.1

Table 18.1 lists concealed-carry studies and whether they found a significant effect. Its columns are left-aligned, so we give pdf_read_table() column edges (relative to the table’s own left margin) rather than centres:

t181 <- pdf_read_table(
  pdf, "18.1", page = 397, header_first = "^Study$",
  edges = c(0, 121), stop_pat = "^(NOTE|SOURCE|a|b)$",
  col_names = c("study", "significant_effect")
)
t181$study <- pdf_strip_footnote_letter(t181$study)
dtab(t181)

A numeric table with a confidence interval: A.3

Table A.3 reports incidence-rate ratios with 95% CIs as a single text column ("1.12 [1.03-1.21]"); once extracted, ordinary regex parsing pulls out the numbers:

a3 <- pdf_read_table(
  pdf, "A.3", page = 492, header_first = "^Study$",
  edges = c(0, 131, 228, 322),
  col_names = c("study", "policy", "outcome", "irr_ci")
)
m <- regmatches(a3$irr_ci, regexec("^([0-9.]+) \\[([0-9.]+)[\u2013-]([0-9.]+)\\]$", a3$irr_ci))
a3[c("irr", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")] <- lapply(2:4, function(i) as.numeric(vapply(m, function(z) z[i], "")))
a3$ci_excludes_1 <- a3$ci_lo > 1 | a3$ci_hi < 1
stopifnot(nrow(a3) == 18, !anyNA(a3$irr))
dtab(a3)

A table where records aren’t separated by whitespace: A.6

Table A.6 compares 2022-vs-2024 conclusions by policy; its first column wraps across lines with no blank line between records, so a new record must instead be recognized by a column that’s always filled – here, “No. of Studies” (column 2):

a6 <- pdf_read_table(
  pdf, "A.6", page = 501, header_first = "^Policy$", header_span = c(2, 0),
  edges = c(0, 113, 136, 252, 276), record = "anchor", anchor_col = 2,
  col_names = c("policy", "n_2022", "conclusion_2022", "n_2024", "conclusion_2024")
)
a6$n_2022 <- as.integer(a6$n_2022)
a6$n_2024 <- as.integer(a6$n_2024)
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
dtab(a6)

If you need to extract a table this package hasn’t already seen, pdf_suggest_edges() measures candidate column left-edges directly from the page – shared x-coordinates across several lines are usually column boundaries:

pdf_suggest_edges(pdf, "A.6", page = 501)
#>     x rel n_lines
#> 1  57   0      36
#> 2 170 113      18
#> 3 193 136      32
#> 4 205 148      18
#> 5 309 252      18
#> 6 332 275      26
#> 7 345 288      14

Bibliographic integrity: linking citations to a RAND-style reference list

This report has no single master bibliography: each chapter closes with its own "Chapter N References" list, in RAND’s own citation style (not author-year), while in-text citations in tables and prose are author-year (e.g. "Lott and Mustard (1997)"). Checking bibliographic integrity here means parsing the chapter’s reference list into structured entries, deriving an author-year key for each one, and confirming every in-text citation resolves to exactly one entry.

refs <- rand_parse_chapter_refs(pdf, chapter = 18, chapter_title = "Concealed-Carry Laws")
length(refs)
#> [1] 135
refs_df <- rand_refs_table(refs)
head(refs_df[c("key", "type", "title", "container")])
#>                 key       type
#> 1         Adams2022    article
#> 2 AldrichNelson1984       misc
#> 3     AnejaEtAl2011    article
#> 4     AnejaEtAl2014 techreport
#> 5  AyresDonohue1999    article
#> 6 AyresDonohue2003a    article
#>                                                                                                                     title
#> 1                                                       No Retreat: The Impact of Stand Your Ground Laws on Violent Crime
#> 2                                                                                                      Linear Probability
#> 3            The Impact of Right-to-Carry Laws and the NRC Report: Lessons for the Empirical Evaluation of Law and Policy
#> 4 The Impact of Right to Carry Laws and the NRC Report: The Latest Lessons for the Empirical Evaluation of Law and Policy
#> 5              Nondiscretionary Concealed Weapons Laws: A Case Study of Statistics, Standards of Proof, and Public Policy
#> 6                                                                      Shooting Down the More Guns, Less Crime Hypothesis
#>                           container
#> 1           Criminal Justice Review
#> 2                              <NA>
#> 3 American Law and Economics Review
#> 4                              <NA>
#> 5 American Law and Economics Review
#> 6               Stanford Law Review

Now link Table 18.1’s study column to this reference table:

t181_linked <- rand_link_citations(t181, "study", refs_df)
stopifnot(!anyNA(t181_linked$bib_key))

# one anchor id per row, so each study links down to its bibliography
# entry and that entry can link back up to this exact row
cite_id <- paste0("cite-", t181_linked$bib_key, "-", seq_len(nrow(t181_linked)))
disp <- t181_linked[c("study", "significant_effect", "bib_key")]
disp$study <- bib_cite_link(t181_linked$bib_key, label = t181_linked$study, id = cite_id)
dtab(disp, escape = FALSE)

Every one of the 22 studies in Table 18.1 resolves to exactly one chapter-18 reference-list entry – the stopifnot() above is the integrity check: if some future edit to the report, or some mistake in the transcription, broke that correspondence, this line would fail instead of silently producing a table with dangling citations. Each study cell above is itself a link down to that entry in the rendered bibliography below.

That setup – parse the chapter’s reference list, link a table’s citations against it, and check the link is complete – is the pattern the rest of this package’s bibliography tools build on. The remaining steps (restricting to the studies actually cited by Table 18.1, and attaching a DOI, looked up via [rand_crossref_doi()] against Crossref and cached in the package so the vignette doesn’t need network access to build) are mechanical, so they’re run but not shown here; only the final rendered bibliography is displayed.

The rendered bibliography

Each entry below links to its DOI on doi.org when one was found via Crossref, or to a plain URL (parsed straight from the reference text) when no DOI was found but a URL was still given; either way, an entry with no DOI is explicitly marked no DOI – a reader should never have to guess whether a missing link means “none exists” or “nobody checked”. The small &uarr; after each entry links back up to the Table 18.1 row that cited it:

cat(rand_bibliography_html(cited, cited_at), sep = "\n")
